entry: American actor, comedian and filmmaker, known for [[Silent film|silent films]]. Keaton, a child [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] performer, became known for physical comedy and inventive stunts performed with a deadpan expression that earned him the nickname "The Great Stone Face." His feature films of the 1920s include *Our Hospitality* (1923), *Sherlock Jr.* (1924) and *The General* (1926), which [[Orson Welles]] called "the greatest comedy ever made." After he signed with [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] in 1928, he lost his artistic independence, and the studio fired him in 1933. In the 1940s he worked as a comic performer, with cameos in Billy Wilder's *Sunset Boulevard* (1950) and [[Charlie Chaplin]]'s *Limelight* (1952).

Flammable [[Alkane|alkane]] hydrocarbon with the formula C₄H₁₀. Butane has two isomers, n-butane and isobutane, both highly flammable, colorless gases that liquefy easily. It is a trace component of [[Natural gas|natural gas]]. Liquefied petroleum gas is a mixture of [[Propane|propane]] and some butanes. Its name derives from *butyric acid*, which is named after the Greek word for butter. Although first synthesized in 1849 and identified in crude petroleum in 1864, butane had little practical use until the 1910s. It is used for [[Gasoline|gasoline]] blending, as a fuel gas, and as a feedstock for [[Ethylene|ethylene]] and butadiene, a key ingredient of synthetic rubber. Complete combustion produces [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and water vapor, while limited oxygen can produce [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] or [[Soot|soot]].

Dairy product made from the fat and protein of churned cream. It is a semi-solid [[Emulsion|emulsion]] at room temperature, containing approximately 81% butterfat, and it melts at 32 to 35 °C (90 to 95 °F). Butter is used as a spread, melted as a condiment, and as a fat in baking, sauce-making and frying. Most butter is made from [[Milk|cow's milk]], though the milk of sheep, goats, buffalo and yaks is also used. Salt has been added since antiquity to help preserve it. Clarified butter, or ghee, is almost entirely butterfat. In 2023, world production of butter made from cow milk was six million tonnes, led by the United States with 16% of the total.

Winged insect of the [[Lepidoptera|lepidopteran]] superfamily Papilionoidea, usually with large, brightly colored wings. Butterflies undergo complete [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]] through four stages: egg, caterpillar (larva), chrysalis (pupa) and adult. They are divided into seven families containing about 20,000 species. Many species use [[Camouflage|camouflage]], mimicry and aposematism to evade predators, and some, such as the [[Monarch butterfly|monarch]], migrate over long distances. Caterpillars of some species damage crops or trees, while adults of other species are agents of [[Pollination|pollination]]. The oldest butterfly fossils date to the Paleocene, about 56 million years ago, though molecular evidence suggests the group originated in the [[Cretaceous]].

Concept in [[Chaos theory|chaos theory]] of sensitive dependence on initial conditions. A small change in the state of a deterministic nonlinear system can cause large differences in a later state. Edward Norton Lorenz, a meteorologist, found the effect when rounded initial data made his weather model diverge from unrounded runs. His 1972 presentation, which used a [[Butterfly|butterfly]] flapping its wings to influence a [[Tornado|tornado]], gave the phrase its name.

Variety of winter squash (*Cucurbita moschata*) with tan skin and orange flesh. Botanically a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], it is used as a vegetable, roasted, puréed into soup, or mashed into casseroles, breads and pies. Its flesh deepens in color as it ripens, owing to its beta-carotene content. The modern variety was developed in 1944 by Charles Leggett of Stow, Massachusetts, who crossed [[Pumpkin|pumpkin]] and gooseneck squash varieties. In Australia and New Zealand it is called butternut pumpkin. The seeds are edible and can be roasted or pressed into an oil.

Pair of rounded fleshy structures on the posterior of the human pelvis, between the lower back and the perineum. Each consists of skin and subcutaneous fat over the gluteus maximus and gluteus medius muscles. The gluteus maximus muscles are the largest in the human body. They straighten the body from a bent position, keep the hip joints extended, and propel the body forward when walking or running. In many cultures the buttocks play a role in [[Sexual attraction|sexual attraction]], and they have been used as a target for corporal punishment because the fat layer protects against injury. Some [[Baboon|baboons]] and all [[Gibbon|gibbons]] have naked ischial callosities, pads that allow primates to sit upright without resting their weight on their feet. Humans lack them because the gluteal muscles provide similar cushioning. The Latin name is *nates*.

Small [[Fastener|fastener]] that joins two pieces of fabric by slipping through a loop or buttonhole. Modern buttons are commonly made of plastic, though metal, wood and seashell are also used, and they may be sewn on purely as ornaments. Button-like ornaments appeared in the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2800–2600 BC), and buttons used as apparel have been found at Bronze Age sites in China and in ancient Rome. Buttonholes for fastening clothing first appeared in 13th-century Germany, and button-making guilds were established in the 13th century. During the [[Renaissance]], buttons of precious metal and jewels became luxury items that signified wealth and status.

American former astronaut, aeronautical engineer and fighter pilot. As lunar module pilot of [[Apollo 11]] in 1969, he became the second person to walk on the Moon, after [[Neil Armstrong]]. He made three spacewalks on the 1966 Gemini 12 mission. After retiring from the U.S. Air Force in 1972, he advocated human missions to Mars and developed the Aldrin cycler, a spacecraft trajectory that makes travel to Mars more efficient in time and propellant.

Unit of digital information, most commonly consisting of eight bits. Historically, a byte was the number of bits used to encode a single character of text, and it is the smallest addressable unit of memory in many computer architectures. Sizes from 1 to 48 bits have been used, but eight bits became the de facto standard because a byte can then represent the values 0 through 255. Network protocol documents such as the [[Internet Protocol|Internet Protocol]] call an 8-bit byte an octet. Werner Buchholz coined the term in June 1956 during the design of the [[IBM]] Stretch computer, respelling "bite" to avoid confusion with [[Bit|bit]].

Series of decisive conflicts between the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] Greeks and [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] Turks, 1299–1453. They led to the final destruction of the Byzantine Empire and the rise of the Ottoman Empire. After [[Constantinople]] was retaken from the Latin Empire in 1261, the Turks under [[Osman I]] began raids into Byzantine Anatolia. Within 90 years of Osman I's founding of the Ottoman principality, the Byzantines had lost all their Anatolian territory, and by 1400 Byzantine Thrace was also lost. [[Timur]]'s invasion in 1402 allowed the ruined city to hold out until it fell to [[Mehmed II]] in 1453, which formally ended the conflicts. Several Byzantine holdouts lasted until 1479. The conquest helped lead to the end of the [[Middle Ages]] and the beginning of the [[Age of Discovery]].

Architecture of the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire, dated from AD 330 to 1453. It was stylistically indistinguishable from late Roman architecture at first, and it relied on [[Arch|arches]], vaults and [[Dome|domes]], often on a large scale. The grandest buildings had gold-background wall mosaics, and rich interiors used thin plates of marble. Churches typically had high-riding domes that heightened the light, and the round arch was fundamental to the style. The style spread west to [[Ravenna]] and [[Venice]] and as far north as [[Moscow]]. The [[Hagia Sophia]] in [[Constantinople]] remained the iconic church of Christianity, and Byzantine architecture influenced later medieval architecture across Europe and the Near East.

American commercial broadcast television and radio network, one of the Big Three television networks. Founded in 1927 as a radio network, it was renamed the Columbia Broadcasting System by William S. Paley, who became its majority owner in 1928. [[Paramount Pictures]] acquired 49 percent of the network in 1929, but the [[Great Depression]] forced the studio to sell its shares back in 1932. The network is headquartered in [[New York City]] and is the flagship property of the CBS Entertainment Group division of Skydance.

Intergovernmental organization operating the world's largest particle physics laboratory. Established in 1954 with 25 member states, it is based in Meyrin, a suburb of [[Geneva]] on the France–Switzerland border. Its [[Large Hadron Collider|Large Hadron Collider]] (LHC) is the world's largest and highest-energy particle collider, and experiments at the LHC observed the [[Higgs boson]] in 2012. CERN is also the birthplace of the [[World Wide Web]].

Standard color space defined by the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) in 1931. It models a "standard observer" of normal human [[Color vision|color vision]]. It was created from color-matching experiments in the mid-1920s by William David Wright and John Guild. A mixture of two colors lies on the straight line between them, but the space is not perceptually uniform, a limitation addressed by later models such as CIELAB. It remains the foundation of modern color models and is a fundamental tool for measuring color in industries including inks, dyes and paints.

Subtractive color model used in color printing, with four [[Ink|inks]]: [[Cyan|cyan]], [[Magenta|magenta]], [[Yellow|yellow]] and black, the key plate. Inks reduce the light reflected from a white substrate such as paper, and black results from combining them. Black ink improves the precision of outlines and text, reduces ink consumption and drying time, and produces more consistent dark tones. Halftoning varies the size and spacing of dots to produce intermediate tones; 20% magenta coverage, for example, produces a pink tone. Unlike [[RGB color model|RGB]] displays, which emit light, CMYK has a more limited gamut, and conversion between the two requires color management profiles because no universal formula exists. CMYK printing was first implemented in the 1890s for color newspaper illustrations and comic strips.

American [[News media|news media]] company and cable news channel, headquartered in [[Atlanta]], Georgia. Founded on June 1, 1980, by [[Ted Turner]] and Reese Schonfeld, it was the first channel to provide 24-hour news coverage. As of December 2023, CNN had 68,974,000 U.S. television households as subscribers, according to Nielsen, down from 80 million in March 2021. Conservative media have criticized CNN for a perceived left-wing bias, while others have criticized it for false balance in support of conservative positions.

Compiled, English-like [[Programming language|programming language]] designed for business use. Its design began in 1959 under CODASYL, partly based on [[Grace Hopper]]'s FLOW-MATIC, and it was standardized in 1968. Statements use prose syntax, such as MOVE x TO y, but the language uses over 300 reserved words and has been criticized as verbose. It has been [[Object-oriented programming|object-oriented]] since 2002. COBOL is still widely used on mainframe computers for large-scale batch and transaction processing, though most programming in it today maintains existing applications.

Series of covert and illegal projects by the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]], conducted from 1956 to 1971 to surveil and disrupt domestic political groups. Targets included civil rights and Black power activists such as [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] and [[Malcolm X]], the [[Black Panther Party]], anti-war New Left groups, and white supremacist groups such as the [[Ku Klux Klan]]. Methods included forged documents, false media reports and harassment. FBI director [[J. Edgar Hoover]] ordered agents to "expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize" these movements. The program became public in 1971, when activists burglarized an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, and disseminated over 1,000 documents.

Contagious disease caused by the [[Coronavirus|coronavirus]] [[SARS-CoV-2]], first identified in [[Wuhan]], China, in December 2019. Symptoms often include fever, fatigue, cough, shortness of breath, and loss of smell or taste, and they may begin 1–14 days after exposure. At least a third of infected people develop no noticeable symptoms. Among patients, 81% have mild to moderate illness, 14% severe illness and 5% critical illness, such as [[Respiratory failure|respiratory failure]] or [[Shock (circulatory)|shock]]. Older people are at higher risk of severe disease, and some people have persistent symptoms, known as [[Long COVID]]. Transmission occurs when infectious particles are breathed in or contact the eyes, nose or mouth. Vaccines have been approved and distributed in many countries.

Global outbreak of [[COVID-19]], beginning in [[Wuhan]], China, in December 2019. The World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern on January 30, 2020, and assessed the outbreak as a pandemic on March 11. Measures included travel restrictions, lockdowns, business closures and mask mandates. Vaccines reached the general public from December 2020, through programs including COVAX. The pandemic caused the largest global recession since the [[Great Depression]]. The WHO declared the public health emergency over on May 5, 2023, while noting that COVID-19 remained a global health threat.

Family of [[DNA|DNA]] sequences found in the genomes of [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]] such as [[Bacteria|bacteria]] and [[Archaea|archaea]]. Each sequence derives from a fragment of a bacteriophage that infected the organism, and it helps detect and destroy DNA from similar viruses, providing heritable immunity. CRISPR is found in approximately 50% of sequenced bacterial genomes and nearly 90% of sequenced archaea. The [[Enzyme|enzyme]] Cas9 uses CRISPR sequences as a guide to recognize and open specific DNA strands, forming the basis of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing. Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing it.

American police procedural drama television series that aired on [[CBS]] from 2000 to 2015. It is the first series in the *CSI* franchise. Its investigators with the [[Las Vegas|Las Vegas]] Metropolitan Police Department use physical evidence to solve murders. It won six Primetime Emmy Awards and was CBS's most successful series at the time. It drew criticism from public officials and law enforcement for its depiction of crimes and graphic content. The follow-up, *CSI: Vegas*, ran for 3 seasons from 2021 to 2024.

Style sheet language that specifies the presentation of documents written in [[HTML|HTML]], XML or similar markup languages. CSS is a cornerstone technology of the [[World Wide Web|World Wide Web]], alongside HTML and [[JavaScript|JavaScript]]. It separates content from presentation, covering layout, [[Color|colors]] and fonts, so that many pages can share one cached style sheet and the same markup can be presented on screen, in print, by speech or on Braille devices. Håkon Wium Lie proposed it in 1994 while working at [[CERN|CERN]]. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) maintains its specifications.

Medical imaging technique that uses X-rays to produce cross-sectional images of the body. A rotating X-ray tube and a row of detectors in a gantry measure how different tissues attenuate X-rays, and a computer reconstructs the measurements from many angles into slice images. Although used mainly in [[Medical diagnosis|medical diagnosis]], CT can also image nonliving objects. Patients with metallic implants or pacemakers may be scanned by CT when [[Magnetic resonance imaging|MRI]] is contraindicated. Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for computer-assisted tomography.
